tags.gist: Wants postmarket monitoring with sample-based clinician review, rates at which nurses or physicians override outputs, and performance broken out by chronic-care subgroup.
Closes with simple principles: licensed judgment stays accountable, risk is autonomy times harm, and the deployed system must prove competent.
Sees nursing assessment as the safest first home for clinical AI, with care-plan drafts bound to patient data and signed off by a nurse.
Says the technology is already in workflows, so the safest step is writing its tests in public and plain language now.
Proposes a nursing body score tools on intended-use honesty, autonomy, contestability, equity testing and monitoring, and publish the results.
Proposes a non-punitive registry of AI-related near misses in nursing workflows, like existing patient-safety organizations.
Adopts the two axes but adds explicit modifiers: reversibility, time to detection, and whether a licensed professional must authenticate the output.
Wants sponsors of documentation and care-plan generators to benchmark the product users actually see, prompts, retrieval and escalation rules included.
Would treat care-plan generators as informational devices or non-device decision support only if they cannot initiate orders or emit a medical diagnosis.
Wants competency evidence on high-consequence recognition tasks chronic-care tools face, such as decompensated heart failure, withdrawal and suicidal ideation.
Places a nurse-authenticated care-plan generator as informational to action-directing, with mandatory authentication and interruptive escalation mitigating consequences.
Argues existing nursing bodies' AI statements are necessary but not sufficient, so a dedicated AI nursing association is needed.
Describes the association's purpose: practice standards for nursing AI, credentialing, docket comments and an evidence registry of evaluated tools.
Wants generators bound to current practice guidelines, citing the clause used, and escalating rather than improvising when none applies.
Cites comparisons of nurse-written and model care plans: time-saving drafts with characteristic errors, supporting a supervised generator over an unsupervised author.
Would keep draft and authenticated plan with a version stamp of model, prompts and guideline library, so review can measure unchanged acceptance.
Says fully autonomous diagnosis should be rare and paired with heightened competency evidence and postmarket surveillance.
Allocates duties: manufacturers for design, validation and change control; facilities for selection, integration and monitoring; clinicians for appropriate use.
Warns a generator free to invent interventions will invent unsafe ones, so proposed actions should be bound to guidelines and protocols.
Would reserve autonomous classification for narrowly validated, contestable tasks; open-ended generative diagnosis should never default to it.
Describes the AMA Appendix S taxonomy of assistive, augmentative and autonomous software, with three autonomous levels by contestability.
Says the two-axis framework maps cleanly onto the Appendix S autonomy taxonomy, with consequence setting each cell's evidence and monitoring.
Gives AI a bounded job in nursing assessment: organize data, compare vital signs to thresholds and draft diagnoses and plans for a nurse.
Says the machine must not make a medical diagnosis, silently drop findings, or treat a draft plan as live before a nurse authenticates it.
Would feed accepted and rejected proposals, de-identified, into local quality review, rather than letting the model silently retrain on identified records without governance.
Keeps physician decision-making with the physician; AI may cut documentation burden and retrieve guidelines but cannot be the attending of record.
Would default documentation tools to assistive and diagnostic support such as risk scores to augmentative, with documented clinician use.
Offers simple principles described as consistent with nursing bodies' positions, the Appendix S taxonomy and FDA's two-axis view.
Principle that a licensed professional stays responsible for what enters the legal record; software may only draft, score or recommend.
Wants intended use stated at the lowest defensible autonomy level, so a documentation assistant is not marketed as a diagnostician.
Agrees risk equals autonomy times harm, so reversible, contestable outputs need less burden than action-directing or autonomous ones.
Agrees the deployed system, with prompts, retrieval, guardrails and interface, is the unit of evaluation, not the model alone.
Wants human review treated as a designed control: contestability, override, escalation and an audit trail of who accepted or rejected outputs.
Wants performance examined across age, sex, race and ethnicity where relevant, language, disability and care setting, as a safety requirement.
Says the professions need standing organizations to set competencies, comment on dockets and keep vendors from capturing clinical language.
Argues nursing assessment is the right first place for clinical AI, being structured, repeated and assistable without claiming medical diagnosis.
Wants the gap between a note-drafting scribe and a diagnosis-recommending system forced into intended-use statements, oversight design and monitoring.
States the governing idea that AI may inform, organize and scale clinical work but not replace licensed judgment or accountable human review.
